items.name: Carbon monoxide (CO) alarm, battery or battery backup
items.need: CO is invisible and odorless, and a power outage or a gas or generator problem can make it dangerous; an alarm is the only warning you get.
items.how_to_choose: Look for UL 2034 on the alarm or its box, and keep the box so you can show it. Battery-powered or battery-backup units keep working in a blackout. A sealed 10-year battery means no battery changes and no battery to forget. Digital displays are useful because they show a reading before the alarm sounds. In a rental, check the lease first: some landlords must supply alarms.

qty.note: One on each level of the home and one outside each sleeping area; add more if your home is large or has several bedroom areas. Where a combination smoke and CO alarm already covers a spot, it needs no separate CO alarm.

items.already_own: A CO alarm you already have is fine if it says UL 2034 on the label, has not passed its end-of-life date (check the back for a replace-by date, or the unit chirps end-of-life), and passes the test button. If it has no date or is older than the maker's stated life, replace it.

safety_notes.text: CPSC says to put CO alarms on every level of the home and outside sleeping areas, to test them monthly, and notes that battery-operated alarms or alarms with battery backup are acceptable. The page does not state when to replace the alarm itself, so follow the maker's end-of-life date or chirp.

items.name: Combination smoke and carbon monoxide (CO) alarm, UL 217 and UL 2034
items.need: One alarm that warns of both smoke and carbon monoxide, so the hallway outside the bedrooms and each level of the home need one unit instead of two.
items.how_to_choose: Choose a photoelectric combination; this page does not pick ionization-only or dual-sensor combinations. Look for UL 217 (smoke) and UL 2034 (CO) on the alarm or its box, and buy a well-known brand from the maker or a major retailer. Where you can, choose alarms that interconnect, by wire or wirelessly, so that when one sounds they all sound; CPSC and the US Fire Administration both recommend this. When a combination unit fails or reaches its end date, both protections go at once, so replace it on the date printed on it, or sooner if its end-of-life warning sounds. In a rental, ask the landlord first, and never remove or disable a hard-wired alarm.

qty.note: One outside each sleeping area and one on each level of the home, in place of a separate smoke alarm and CO alarm in those spots. Bedrooms still need their own smoke alarms.

items.already_own: A combination alarm you already have is fine if its label says UL 217 and UL 2034, it passes the test button, it is not chirping an end-of-life warning, and it has not passed the replace-by date on its back. A working smoke alarm and a working CO alarm already in the same spot do the same job; there is no need to swap them for one combination unit.

safety_notes.text: CPSC says to buy only combination smoke and CO detectors that meet both UL 2034 and UL 217, to install them on each level of the home and outside separate sleeping areas, and to choose ones that run on batteries or have battery backup.

items.need: Most fatal home fires happen when people are asleep; a working alarm gives you the minutes you need to get out.
items.how_to_choose: Look for UL 217 on the box. A sealed 10-year battery removes battery changes; the whole alarm is replaced at 10 years. Photoelectric sensors handle smoldering fires and fewer cooking false alarms. In a rented apartment the landlord usually has to provide working alarms, so ask them first, and never remove or disable a hard-wired alarm; add battery alarms in addition, only where allowed. Alarms that interconnect, by wire or wirelessly, all sound when one does; CPSC prefers them, and they matter most where bedroom doors are kept shut. None of the picks below interconnects.

items.already_own: An alarm you already have is fine if it passes the test button, is under 10 years old (check the manufacture date on the back) and is not yellowed or chirping. Replace anything 10 years or older.

safety_notes.text: NFPA says to put smoke alarms in every bedroom, outside sleeping areas and on each level, to test them monthly, and to replace them after about ten years. It also mentions sealed batteries.

items.name: Home fire extinguisher (ABC dry chemical, UL rated)
items.need: A small kitchen or appliance fire can be stopped in its first seconds, but only if the right extinguisher is within reach and you know when to use it and when to leave.
items.how_to_choose: Buy a multipurpose ABC extinguisher with a UL rating of at least 1-A:10-B:C; 2-A:10-B:C or 3-A:40-B:C is better. Pick one you can lift and carry easily. Prefer rechargeable models with a metal valve and a pressure gauge; avoid plastic-valve or plastic-handle disposables. Keep it near the kitchen exit, not next to the stove, and learn the PASS steps.

qty.note: One for the kitchen side of the home; add one per floor of a multi-floor home.

items.already_own: An extinguisher you already own is fine if the gauge needle is in the green, the pin and seal are intact, it is not dented or corroded, and it is not a recalled Kidde plastic-handle model. Check the Kidde recall ID guide and CPSC recall 18-022 if yours is Kidde.

safety_notes.text: USFA says to use an extinguisher only if you have alerted others, the fire department has been called, you are able to use it, the fire is small and limited to one object, you are protected from toxic smoke, and you have a clear way out. If any of this is uncertain, leave, and call 911 from outside or a neighbor's phone. Multipurpose A-B-C extinguishers cover most home fires.
safety_notes.source_title: Choosing and Using Fire Extinguishers

safety_notes.text: USFA's PASS steps: pull the pin with the nozzle pointed away from you, aim at the base of the fire, squeeze the handle slowly and evenly, and sweep side to side.
safety_notes.source_title: Choosing and Using Fire Extinguishers

items.name: Kitchen fire blanket
items.need: Some fire services abroad suggest a fire blanket for a small oil or fat fire in a pan, but US fire bodies give no advice on them and Ontario's fire marshal does not endorse them for home use, so this site suggests a pan lid by the stove instead.
items.how_to_choose: This site does not suggest buying one. If you choose to, look for a certificate from a testing body naming the standard: in Europe that is EN 1869:2019, in Australia AS/NZS 3504:2006, and the US standard for cooking fire suppression blankets is ASTM F1989. A maker saying a blanket meets a standard is not the same as a certificate, so ask for the certificate. Pick one in a wall-mounted case you can mount by the kitchen door.

qty.note: Optional. At most one, on the wall near the kitchen door; a pan lid by the stove comes first.

items.already_own: Keep a fire blanket you already own on the wall near the kitchen door, not beside the stove or under the sink, and replace it after any use on a real fire. A blanket with no standard named on it is not a tool to count on; keep a pan lid by the stove either way.

safety_notes.text: For a pan fire, the US Fire Administration says to keep a pan lid or baking sheet nearby and slide it over the pan, and to turn off the burner if grease starts to smoke or boil. It does not mention fire blankets.
safety_notes.source_title: Cooking fire safety

safety_notes.text: Ontario's fire marshal does not endorse fire blankets for household use, says only trained professionals should use them, and notes that no Canadian standard covers them. For a small grease fire, slide a lid over the pan and turn off the burner.
safety_notes.source_title: Pickering Fire Services cautions against fire blankets, urges focus on proven fire safety measures

safety_notes.text: London Fire Brigade says not to tackle a pan fire yourself, not to move the pan and never to use water; switch off the heat only if safe, then get out, shut the door and call for help.
safety_notes.source_title: Pan fires

safety_notes.text: South Australia's fire service recommends a blanket meeting AS/NZS 3504:2006, mounted near a door out of the kitchen. It is lowered over the pan, never thrown, with a lid or tray put on top, the heat turned off and the pan left to cool for at least an hour. Never carry a burning pan, and replace the blanket after use.
safety_notes.source_title: Fire Blankets (fact sheet)

items.name: Plastic sheeting and duct tape (room sealing)
items.need: Heavy plastic sheeting and tape let you cover the windows, door gaps and vents of one room for the few hours officials may tell you to shelter from a chemical release outside.
items.how_to_choose: Buy clear polyethylene sheeting that the maker states is 4 mil or thicker; 6 mil tears less when you tape and re-tape it. Pick the room first: it needs at least 10 square feet of floor for each person. Measure its windows, vents and door, and cut each sheet several inches larger than its opening. Choose a cloth-backed rubber-adhesive duct tape. A 10 ft by 25 ft roll is easy to store in an apartment closet.

qty.note: One roll of sheeting and one roll of tape for one room; measure the openings first and add more for a large room or many windows.

items.already_own: Any sheeting you already own is fine if it is clear polyethylene of 4 mil or thicker with no holes. Painter's drop cloths thinner than 4 mil are too weak. Any duct tape that still sticks well is fine; old rolls dry out, so test it.

safety_notes.text: Ready.gov describes sealing windows, doors and air vents with thick plastic sheeting and duct tape as a temporary protective measure against contaminated outside air, and tells people to follow local authorities and keep the materials in their supply kit.
safety_notes.source_title: Shelter | Ready.gov

safety_notes.text: FEMA's figure is 10 square feet of floor for each person: that gives enough air to stop carbon dioxide building up for up to 5 hours at rest. FEMA adds that many chemical releases thin out within a few hours.
safety_notes.source_title: How long to remain in shelter-in-place room?

safety_notes.text: CDC says to tape plastic sheeting over the windows, close and tape over any vents, and tape round the door, and to stay until police, fire or other local officials give the all clear. CDC describes pre-cut plastic sheets 2 to 4 mil thick; this page picks 4 mil or thicker because it tears less. CDC also says an order to stay put can last a few hours or, sometimes, days.
safety_notes.source_title: What to Do to Shelter in Place for a Chemical Emergency

safety_notes.text: For smoke, which is a different job from a chemical release, EPA's clean-room page says to close windows and doors without making it hard to get out, and to air the room out when the air outside improves, even for a short time.
safety_notes.source_title: Create a Clean Room to Protect Indoor Air Quality During a Wildfire

item_flags: A sealed room is for a few hours. It holds only the air that was in it when you sealed it: use a room with at least 10 square feet (about 1 square meter) of floor for each person, which on FEMA's figure gives enough air for up to 5 hours at rest. An order to stay indoors for longer, which CDC says can last days, means windows shut and ventilation off, not living in the taped room.
Do not seal in a way that blocks your exit, and never burn fuel, run a generator or use a gas stove or heater in a sealed room.
items.tier_note: One pick: sheeting and duct tape are much alike, and a pricier roll buys nothing the job needs; buy a second roll if you have many windows.

items.name: Portable HEPA air cleaner for one bedroom-size clean room
items.need: When outdoor smoke or dust gets inside, a HEPA air cleaner in one closed room is the main way to keep that room's air cleaner.
items.how_to_choose: Choose a true-HEPA unit and match its smoke CADR (clean air delivery rate) and the maker's stated room size to the room you will use. Check that the exact model is on the California Air Resources Board (CARB) list: a listing means the unit passed an electrical safety test and, if it has electronic parts such as an ionizer, stays under California's ozone limit. It says nothing about how well the unit cleans. Never buy an ozone generator or a unit with an ionizer you cannot turn off, and leave an ionizer switched off. Run it on high in the closed room if the noise is tolerable.

qty.note: One for the room you will use as a clean room, usually a bedroom.

items.already_own: A true-HEPA unit you already own is fine if its filter is fresh, it is rated for your room and it is not an ozone generator or an ionizer-only device. Leave any ionizer switched off. Replace a dirty filter before heavy smoke.

safety_notes.text: EPA says to choose a portable air cleaner sized for the room, run it continuously on high if possible, pick one that does not make ozone, and use CARB's list of tested devices. It also says to keep the room's windows and doors closed without blocking your exit, avoid smoke-making activities indoors, and change filters more often in heavy smoke.
safety_notes.source_title: Create a Clean Room to Protect Indoor Air Quality During a Wildfire

safety_notes.text: California's Air Resources Board says every air cleaner on its certified list has been tested for electrical safety, and that electronic air cleaners must also meet an ozone limit of 0.050 parts per million. It says its certification does not reflect how effective an air cleaner is.

safety_notes.text: Virginia's Department of Health says not to use a system with an ionizer or an ozone setting unless you can turn it off, because these settings can make chemicals that irritate the lungs. Washington State's Department of Health says to choose filters only and avoid ionizer, ozone and ultraviolet technologies.
safety_notes.source_title: Keeping Indoor Air Clean During Wildfires

safety_notes.text: EPA says air cleaners that contain ionizers or electrostatic precipitators can give off ozone in some cases, that ozone irritates the lungs, and that the CADR rating is for particles only, not gases.

items.name: DIY box-fan air cleaner kit (20 in fan + 20x20 MERV 13 filters)
items.need: A box fan with a furnace filter taped to it is a low-cost way to clean the air in one room when a commercial air cleaner is not available or affordable.
items.how_to_choose: Use a 20 inch box fan made in 2012 or later with a UL or ETL mark, plus 20x20 MERV 13 filters. Tape the filter to the back (intake) side so the airflow arrow points into the fan, and seal all four edges. More filters (for example a four-filter cube) clean the air faster than one. Replace filters when dirty.

qty.note: One fan and one filter set for one small room.

items.already_own: A 20 inch box fan made in 2012 or later that carries a UL or ETL mark, plus a MERV 13 furnace filter, is enough. Avoid a fan made before 2012, and do not use a filter that is heavily loaded.

safety_notes.text: EPA's DIY air cleaner page describes a 20 x 20 inch box fan with a 20 x 20 inch filter (1 or 4 inch) attached to the back, filter arrow pointing into the fan. It says to use a 2012 or later fan with safety features such as fused plugs and thermal cutoffs, and only fans carrying a UL or ETL marking. A 2021 UL and EPA study found no burn or fire risk in the conditions tested. Dirty filters loaded with smoke or dust were almost useless in EPA lab tests, so replace them. Designs with more MERV 13 filters did better.
safety_notes.source_title: Do-It-Yourself Air Cleaners: Making Cleaner Air More Accessible

safety_notes.text: EPA says to use only a 2012-or-later fan with a UL or ETL mark, and that a fan built before 2012 must not be left unattended or used while you sleep. It also says: no extension cord, do not leave children alone with the fan running, do not use a damaged fan, and have working smoke alarms throughout the home.
safety_notes.source_title: DIY Air Cleaners

safety_notes.text: EPA's research page says fans built before 2012 were not tested and pose known fire risks. It says to check the filter every day during smoke and to change it when it is dark brown or gray or smells of smoke.
safety_notes.source_title: Research on DIY Air Cleaners to Reduce Wildfire Smoke Indoors

safety_notes.text: CDC says that if you use a do-it-yourself box-fan filter unit, never leave it unattended.
safety_notes.source_title: Safety Guidelines: Wildfires and Wildfire Smoke

safety_notes.text: EPA says commercial air cleaners have more reliable performance testing than DIY ones, and that filters in DIY cleaners may need changing every few weeks or every few days in heavy smoke.
safety_notes.source_title: Create a Clean Room to Protect Indoor Air Quality During a Wildfire

item_flags: CDC says never to leave a home-made unit running unattended. EPA says to use only a 2012-or-later fan with a UL or ETL mark, and that an older fan must never run unattended or while you sleep. This site's rule: run it only while someone is awake in the home.
That rule means this kit is for the hours someone is awake. For the room you sleep in, use a commercial HEPA air cleaner, which EPA says to run continuously.
EPA says to use a home-made air cleaner when a commercial unit is not available or affordable, and names thermal cutoffs as a safety feature of newer fans: a fan that lists one is better.
items.tier_note: Two picks: spending more buys a commercial HEPA air cleaner, which can run while you sleep (see the HEPA air cleaner).
